title: The Prompt Payment Discount: What Two Percent Off Is Really Costing Your Margin
excerpt: A two percent early payment discount feels free because nobody costs it like a loan. Run the maths and it often implies a rate several times what a bank would charge for the same cash.
content:
A lot of owner-led businesses offer a discount for early payment without ever running the number on what it actually costs. Two percent off for settling within ten days instead of the usual thirty feels like a fair trade, a little less revenue for a little more certainty about when the money lands. Because it is labelled a discount rather than a cost, it rarely gets costed the way every other line in the business does.

The terms usually are not designed so much as inherited. They sit on an old invoice template, or they were copied from a supplier's own terms years ago, and nobody has looked at them since. Meanwhile the business has grown, the margin has shifted, and the cash position that made the discount sensible in the first place may no longer be the one the business is actually in.

None of this means early payment discounts are wrong. It means they are a financial decision wearing the costume of a customer service gesture, and like any financial decision, they are worth running through the numbers rather than running on habit.

Why the Discount Feels Free

Discounts like this rarely show up anywhere that gets watched closely. They are netted off the invoice before it is recorded, so instead of appearing as a single, visible cost the business can weigh against a benefit, it dissolves into slightly lower revenue, spread thin across hundreds of invoices over a year. Nobody treats it as a finance cost, even though that is exactly what it is: the price paid for access to cash sooner.

Compare that to the way the same business would treat a loan. A bank facility comes with a rate, a term and a repayment schedule that gets reviewed at least once a year. An early payment discount comes with none of that scrutiny, despite functioning the same way: trading a known amount of money today for a smaller amount later, except in reverse, trading a slice of revenue for cash sooner.

What Two Percent Actually Costs

Run the maths on a typical case and the number is usually larger than it looks. Say a business offers two percent off for payment within ten days against standard terms of thirty days. The business is paying for access to that cash twenty days earlier. Annualised, trading away two percent of an invoice's value to bring the payment forward by twenty days works out to an implied cost of money well above thirty percent a year, several multiples higher than what the same business would pay a bank for an overdraft or a line of credit covering the same gap.

The comparison gets sharper once it is run against margin rather than revenue. On a business holding a ten percent net margin, a two percent discount on an invoice is not costing two percent of revenue. It is costing a fifth of the profit sitting in that sale, handed over for the sake of being paid a few weeks sooner. Multiply that across every invoice where a customer takes the discount, and a line item nobody has looked at since the terms were set can be quietly taking a meaningful bite out of annual profit.

When It Is Worth Keeping, and When It Is Not

None of this is an argument for scrapping every early payment discount. For a business that is genuinely cash constrained, paying a premium for faster access to cash can be the right call, the same way paying a higher interest rate for short-term finance can be the right call when the alternative is missing payroll or a supplier deadline. The difference is that decision should be made deliberately, with the real cost in view, rather than defaulting to a discount because it has always been offered.

It is also worth separating two different problems that an early payment discount often gets used to solve at once: a genuine cash timing gap, and a debtor base that pays slowly because the terms and collections process have never been tightened. A structured reset of invoicing, terms and the collections process usually does more to fix slow payment than a discount does, because it changes the behaviour causing the delay instead of paying to work around it on every single invoice.

Where a discount is kept, it is worth pricing it the way any other cost gets priced: compared against what a bank facility would charge for the same cash, revisited at least once a year, and withdrawn from customers who were never going to pay slowly in the first place. A term that was set years ago and never revisited is rarely still the right one for the business as it stands today.

Most owner-led businesses carry at least one cost like this: small on any single invoice, inherited rather than decided, and never quite visible enough to make it onto the agenda. Pulling it into the open usually takes nothing more than running the actual numbers and asking whether the terms still earn their place, a conversation that sits comfortably inside the kind of ongoing financial discipline a fractional CFO partnership brings to a growing business.

faqs.q: What does a two percent early payment discount actually cost a business?
faqs.a: More than it looks. Trading two percent of an invoice's value for payment twenty days sooner than standard thirty day terms works out to an implied cost of money well above thirty percent a year, several times what the same business would pay a bank for short-term finance covering the same gap. On a ten percent margin, that two percent is actually a fifth of the profit in the sale.

faqs.q: Is an early payment discount the same thing as a late payment penalty?
faqs.a: No, though they solve a similar problem from opposite directions. A late payment penalty charges a customer more for paying slowly, while an early payment discount pays a customer less to encourage paying quickly. Both are pricing decisions about the cost of cash timing, and both deserve the same scrutiny as any other cost in the business, not a default setting nobody revisits.

faqs.q: Should an Australian SME offer a discount for payment within ten days?
faqs.a: It depends on how genuinely cash constrained the business is and what the discount is actually buying. For a business with a real short-term cash gap, paying for faster access to cash can make sense, and it sits more easily within a business already running a disciplined cash flow rhythm than one papering over a slow-paying debtor book.

faqs.q: How do I work out if my current payment terms are too generous?
faqs.a: Compare what the discount is costing against what a bank facility would charge for the same amount of cash over the same number of days. If the implied cost of the discount is higher than the business's cost of borrowing, which it usually is, the terms are worth revisiting rather than left to run on habit.

faqs.q: What is a reasonable early payment discount for an Australian SME to offer?
faqs.a: There is no single figure that suits every business, because it depends on margin, how cash constrained the business genuinely is, and what a bank facility would cost for the same period. The pattern worth avoiding is a rate copied from an old template years ago and never checked against the business as it stands today.

faqs.q: How can a business reduce debtor days without discounting every invoice?
faqs.a: Tightening invoicing, payment terms and the collections process usually does more than a discount, because it changes the behaviour causing the delay rather than simply paying around it every time. A Debtor and Collections Reset covers terms templates, a structured follow-up workflow and a focused sixty-day collections sprint for debtors already running late.

faqs.q: Does an early payment discount count as a finance cost?
faqs.a: Functionally, yes, even though it is rarely recorded that way. It is netted against revenue before it reaches the profit and loss statement, so it never appears as its own line, but the business is still trading a slice of margin for earlier access to cash, the same trade a loan or overdraft makes in reverse. It is exactly the kind of quiet cost a fractional CFO partnership is built to catch.
